definition: Flaccid means completely loose and floppy — lacking the firmness or strength something is supposed to have.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word flaccid. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know flaccid should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Flaccid means limp and soft — lacking the firmness something should have, like a balloon three days after the party, hanging flaccid and wrinkled from its ribbon.
Soft things yield to pressure but can still hold their shape; flaccid things have lost their firmness completely and droop.
Lifeless goes beyond flaccid — a flaccid stem still has some substance to it, but a lifeless one has nothing left at all.

Limp means without stiffness or firmness right now — a limp handshake, limp lettuce, limp noodles. It is the everyday word. Flaccid means the same physical looseness but sounds clinical and precise, the term a doctor or gardener might use for muscles or stems that have lost their firmness.

Droopy describes things hanging or sagging downward weakly — droopy eyelids, a droopy houseplant. It is about posture: which way something sags. Flaccid is about internal firmness being gone entirely, whatever position the thing is in. A droopy flower bends over; a flaccid stem has no firmness left inside.

Floppy means loose and bending easily — describing things that visibly flop about when moved, like a hat brim, a puppy's ears, or an old paperback's cover. It is casual and a little playful. Flaccid is its clinical cousin: the formal word for tissue or material that has lost the firmness it should have.

Flaccid's -id ending appears in its exact opposite, rigid — Latin built both adjectives with the same '-id' suffix meaning 'in that state.'
Flaccid means completely loose and floppy — lacking the firmness or strength something is supposed to have.
Distracted by a phone call, Nadia boiled the celery far too long, and the once-crisp stalks turned flaccid, drooping over the edge of the plate.
The stalks went from crisp to drooping — a complete loss of the firmness they were supposed to have.
That physical limpness is exactly what flaccid describes.
Physical & slightly formal
Flaccid is mostly literal — muscles, plant stems, balloons, dough that should be firm but isn't.
Writers occasionally stretch it to arguments or prose ('a flaccid essay'), but in everyday speech 'limp' is the natural choice; flaccid sounds clinical.

Rao's biology class began with two bowls of potato slices, one soaking in plain water, one in heavily salted water.
An hour later the difference needed no microscope.
The freshwater slices snapped crisply in half; the salted ones had turned flaccid, folding over a fingertip without any resistance at all.
Salt, she explained, had pulled the water out of the cells, and water pressure was the only thing that had ever held the tissue firm.
The lab notebooks asked for one word to describe the drained slices, and she insisted on the precise one.
